chapters.title: Chapter 1377 The Massacre Begins
paragraphs: Author: The Last chapter has been edited slightly due to some misunderstandings/misinterpretations I saw. The elves are not all lesbians, not at all. The older elves were not trying to force Eilwen to become a lesbian either; they just suggested it, seeing her being lonely. They became angry because she was a rude brat, not because she refused. Thanks for reading, and enjoy the chapters!
Quinlan and his group hovered high in the skies, watching.
Below, the battlefield was in motion.

Undead surged through the lower districts in uneven waves, pushing human defenders out of streets and courtyards that had turned slick with churned dirt and shattered stone. Their movements were ugly but relentless. They climbed over fallen bodies without breaking pace, drawing fire that would have pinned living troops in place.
Outside the walls, the Elvardian army advanced. Dwarven tankers marched at the front, drawing in devastating ranged attacks that would've pulverized those that stood behind them.
On the walls, human defenders scrambled.

Quinlan could see it clearly from above. Crossbow teams rushed into position, hands shaking as they cranked mechanisms that had already overheated once today. Mages leaned over parapets, trying to angle spells downward now that the barrier was gone. Arrows and bolts rained toward the approaching ranks.
Most fell short.
Then the elves answered.

From behind the dwarven lines, volleys rose in brutal arcs. There were no chaotic storms, but clean lines of fire released in staggered timing, each shot placed delicately rather than being thrown and hoping for the best.

Human defenders vanished from the walls in clusters. A figure would rise to aim, then drop out of sight before the string finished vibrating. Spellcasters slumped backward, hands still raised, light fading from unfinished constructs.
Quinlan watched it unfold and let out a slow breath.

"I always knew elves were devastating archers, but seeing this... It puts everything in a new line for me." He'd already seen elven archery, but never a thousand of them standing shoulder to shoulder and releasing pure death in the form of a relentless downpour of devastation.
Sylvaris, the moon mage elf, spoke up suddenly. Her long hair was bound tight for war, and her robes drawn in close so they would not interfere. Her eyes followed the volleys as she explained,

"Elves live long lives. Long enough to repeat the same motion millions of times. Drawing. Anchoring. Release. Correction. Again. Furthermore, we elves are serene, stationary people by nature. This allows us to practice our craft with extraordinary patience. Where members of other races would've grown bored and burned out of repeating the same motions, we feel at peace."
Another volley fell. Another stretch of wall went quiet.

"Most of us have a natural inclination for ranged combat," she continued. "Balance, perception, spatial awareness. When you give people like that thousands of years to train, combined with extreme amounts of patience, you don't get mere archers. You get instruments of death."
Quinlan glanced at her.
She did not look away from the battlefield.
"Faster release cycles," Sylvaris went on. "Tighter groupings. Better judgment of wind, distance, and movement. Other races compensate with numbers or power. We refine."
A ladder reached the wall. Dwarven shock troops rushed up behind their shields. Above them, an elven volley cut down the defenders trying to push the ladder back.
Sylvaris finally allowed herself a small lift of her chin.
"I may be a mage who can't even handle a bow without embarrassing myself, but I am proud of my people."
"And for a good reason," Quinlan nodded with a fond smile. He was amazed by this display as well. Based on the sight, so were most of his allies.
"Now then, ladies. Let's get to work, shall we?"
They answered without words. A shift in stance. A tightening of grips. One by one, they nodded.
Sylvaris spoke again.
"Prodigious Son. I have a suggestion. If we repeat the same strategies too often, our enemies will adapt."
Quinlan turned his head toward her, and he smiled, already aware of what she had in mind.
"I know," he replied. "Go ahead, mother-in-law."

For the briefest moment, she blinked. But no protest followed. Seraphiel might not carry his mark in any formal sense yet, but the bond was already settled in quieter ways. In their hearts, those two have been engaged for months now.
Sylvaris raised both hands.

Silver light gathered around her fingers, dense and controlled, flowing outward in clean lines rather than bursts. The air bent as shapes took form. One after another, constructs assembled themselves. They sported smooth frames of pale magic and wings unfolded from their backs. Winged mounts, long-bodied and stable, built to carry riders rather than for speed alone.
The girls moved without needing instruction.
Each took a seat, balance natural, knees locking in as if they had done this countless times before. They had. This was not a new tactic. It was a practiced one.
Aurora cast next.
She lifted her staff and drew a wide arc through the air. Light spread outward and settled over the group, forming a layered barrier that moved with them.
Flying shock troops.
Fast. Protected. Able to strike, reposition, and strike again before ground forces could respond.
They were incredibly deadly.
Sylvaris lowered her hands as the last construct stabilized.
"See you later, Quin!"
"Have fun becoming the person you want to be!"
"Have no regrets!"
"I love you!"
The girls cheerily said their goodbyes, many blowing him kisses or just offering loving smiles.
Then they leaned forward, mounts angling down, wings biting into the air. In seconds, they peeled away from Quinlan, forming silver shapes that were streaking toward the walls.
Quinlan watched them go until distance swallowed their forms.
Only he remained, hovering with the Black Fang gang at his side.
"Why did she not summon horsies for us?" Vex whimpered. "Such a cruel auntie!"
"Because I told her not to," Quinlan replied with a nonchalant voice.
"Huh? Why did you do that, Hubby?" Vex gasped. "She can create four more horsies easily! It wouldn't tax her too much."

"Because horsies reduce the effectiveness of you four ancient ladies. My girls have been training for combat using Sylvaris's moonlit constructs, but you four have been fighting together for over a hundred years, while Black Fang, Orianna, and Raika have never ridden a horsie like that before."
"You ancient ladies."
That was as far as the sentence got.
As far as the women were concerned, the rest of Quinlan's explanation vanished into the void. Or, rather, it never even existed.
Vex's ears twitched once. Orianna's expression went very still. And Black Fang... The Venomborne Terror in her frame was seeping out.
The women slowly turned their heads toward him.
Their eyes burned with the unified, concentrated fury of offended femininity.
"Ancient?" Vex repeated softly.
Quinlan felt it immediately. The pressure. The silent, suffocating judgment. He cleared his throat.
"What I meant was-"
Too late.
The glares sharpened. Three of them weren't even blinking anymore.
Raika, meanwhile, looked between them, then up at Quinlan, completely unbothered.
"Then what? I hope you don't expect me to sit this one out just because I can't ride horses. If that's the case, you'd better let me down before I begin swinging."
Her raven hair whipped around her face as she leaned forward, eyes bright, fists already clenching. "I hate watching without partaking."
Quinlan's lips curved.
"You, dearest Raika," he said, tone suddenly pleased, "have hit the nail right on the head."
She blinked. "What do you-"

"I always knew elves were devastating archers, but seeing this...

It puts everything in a new line for me." He'd already seen elven archery, but never a thousand of them standing shoulder to shoulder and releasing pure death in the form of a relentless downpour of devastation.
Sylvaris, the moon mage elf, spoke up suddenly.
Her long hair was bound tight for war, and her robes drawn in close so they would not interfere.
Her eyes followed the volleys as she explained,
"Elves live long lives.
Long enough to repeat the same motion millions of times.
Drawing.
Anchoring.
Release.
Correction.
Again.
Furthermore, we elves are serene, stationary people by nature.
This allows us to practice our craft with extraordinary patience.
Where members of other races would've grown bored and burned out of repeating the same motions, we feel at peace."
Another volley fell.
Another stretch of wall went quiet.
"Most of us have a natural inclination for ranged combat," she continued.
"Balance, perception, spatial awareness.
When you give people like that thousands of years to train, combined with extreme amounts of patience, you don't get mere archers.
You get instruments of death."
Quinlan glanced at her.
She did not look away from the battlefield.
"Faster release cycles," Sylvaris went on.
"Tighter groupings.
Better judgment of wind, distance, and movement.
Other races compensate with numbers or power.
We refine."
A ladder reached the wall.
Dwarven shock troops rushed up behind their shields.
Above them, an elven volley cut down the defenders trying to push the ladder back.
Sylvaris finally allowed herself a small lift of her chin.
"I may be a mage who can't even handle a bow without embarrassing myself, but I am proud of my people."
"And for a good reason," Quinlan nodded with a fond smile.
He was amazed by this display as well.
Based on the sight, so were most of his allies.
"Now then, ladies.
Let's get to work, shall we?"
They answered without words.
A shift in stance.
A tightening of grips.
One by one, they nodded.
Sylvaris spoke again.
"Prodigious Son.
I have a suggestion.
If we repeat the same strategies too often, our enemies will adapt."
Quinlan turned his head toward her, and he smiled, already aware of what she had in mind.
"I know," he replied.
"Go ahead, mother-in-law."
For the briefest moment, she blinked.
But no protest followed.
Seraphiel might not carry his mark in any formal sense yet, but the bond was already settled in quieter ways.
In their hearts, those two have been engaged for months now.
Sylvaris raised both hands.
Silver light gathered around her fingers, dense and controlled, flowing outward in clean lines rather than bursts.
The air bent as shapes took form.
One after another, constructs assembled themselves.
They sported smooth frames of pale magic and wings unfolded from their backs.
Winged mounts, long-bodied and stable, built to carry riders rather than for speed alone.
The girls moved without needing instruction.
Each took a seat, balance natural, knees locking in as if they had done this countless times before.
They had.
This was not a new tactic.
It was a practiced one.
Aurora cast next.
She lifted her staff and drew a wide arc through the air.
Light spread outward and settled over the group, forming a layered barrier that moved with them.
Flying shock troops.
Fast.
Protected.
Able to strike, reposition, and strike again before ground forces could respond.
They were incredibly deadly.
Sylvaris lowered her hands as the last construct stabilized.
"See you later, Quin!"
"Have fun becoming the person you want to be!"
"Have no regrets!"
"I love you!"
The girls cheerily said their goodbyes, many blowing him kisses or just offering loving smiles.
Then they leaned forward, mounts angling down, wings biting into the air.
In seconds, they peeled away from Quinlan, forming silver shapes that were streaking toward the walls.
Quinlan watched them go until distance swallowed their forms.
Only he remained, hovering with the Black Fang gang at his side.
"Why did she not summon horsies for us?" Vex whimpered.
"Such a cruel auntie!"
"Because I told her not to," Quinlan replied with a nonchalant voice.
"Huh?
Why did you do that, Hubby?" Vex gasped.
"She can create four more horsies easily!
It wouldn't tax her too much."
"Because horsies reduce the effectiveness of you four ancient ladies.

My girls have been training for combat using Sylvaris's moonlit constructs, but you four have been fighting together for over a hundred years, while Black Fang, Orianna, and Raika have never ridden a horsie like that before."
"You ancient ladies."
That was as far as the sentence got.
As far as the women were concerned, the rest of Quinlan's explanation vanished into the void.
Or, rather, it never even existed.
Vex's ears twitched once.
Orianna's expression went very still.
And Black Fang...
The Venomborne Terror in her frame was seeping out.
The women slowly turned their heads toward him.
Their eyes burned with the unified, concentrated fury of offended femininity.
"Ancient?" Vex repeated softly.
Quinlan felt it immediately.
The pressure.
The silent, suffocating judgment.
He cleared his throat.
"What I meant was-"
Too late.
The glares sharpened.
Three of them weren't even blinking anymore.
Raika, meanwhile, looked between them, then up at Quinlan, completely unbothered.
"Then what?
I hope you don't expect me to sit this one out just because I can't ride horses.
If that's the case, you'd better let me down before I begin swinging."
Her raven hair whipped around her face as she leaned forward, eyes bright, fists already clenching.
"I hate watching without partaking."
Quinlan's lips curved.
"You, dearest Raika," he said, tone suddenly pleased, "have hit the nail right on the head."
She blinked.
"What do you-"

chapters.title: Chapter 1378 New Usage
paragraphs: She blinked. "What do you-"
He didn't let her finish.
Quinlan grabbed all of them with a single burst of force and hurled them forward.
Not gently.
Not one bit.
They became screaming projectiles.
The sky tore past them as the ground rushed up at horrifying speed, wind ripping at cloaks and hair. Raika's eyes went wide for half a second.
Then she laughed.

"That's more like it!" she shouted, slamming her fists together mid-air, joints popping as her body aligned instinctively for impact. Her grin stretched sharply and eagerly. "You're still an arrogant bastard, but we speak the same language!"
Behind her, three other figures twisted in the air with terrifying control.
Despite plummeting at extreme velocity, Vex, Orianna, and Black Fang somehow managed to rotate their bodies enough to keep their eyes locked on Quinlan.
Their expressions were no longer merely offended.
They were lethal.
Quinlan winced.
"Use that hatred to fuel your attacks!" he shouted after them.
The glares intensified.
"Hubby!" Vex shrieked. "No kissing me for a week!"
She crossed her arms beneath her chest in a dramatic pout while still hurtling toward the battlefield like a thrown siege weapon, cheeks puffed.

"A whole week! And I won't change my mind, no matter how you beg or say flowery words! I am a woman who can put her feet down when I am forced to!" she added, just to be sure he understood the gravity of his situation.

"You will fold within minutes, my beloved Hexwitch..." Quinlan chuckled to himself with a satisfied expression, watching as they vanished downward, one grinning demon and three very angry women about to hit the city like divine retribution.
The laughter faded with the departure of the ladies.
The wind thinned. The noise of battle below became distant, muffled by height and focus. Quinlan hovered alone now, the sky empty around him.
His posture changed.
His posture changed.
The looseness bled out of him, inch by inch. Shoulders settled. Spine straightened. Breath slowed until it barely moved his chest. The playful tilt of his mouth vanished, leaving nothing behind it.
"Synchra. Soul Reaper."
The air answered.
Red light bled through the seams of his armor. Plates shifted against one another with a muted grind as internal defensive measures woke. From the pocket ring on his finger, metal screamed.
A dark saber tore free, spinning once before snapping into his grasp. Blue flame crawled along its edge, dense and steady.
Quinlan closed his fingers around the hilt.
The last trace of warmth left his eyes.
Below him, thousands fought and died. To him, it resolved into lines, clusters, vectors. Where undead clogged streets. Where humans retreated in knots. Where pressure points waited to collapse.
He was no longer a man watching a battlefield.
He was a solution moving toward a problem.
And the Primordial Villain began his work.

Quinlan's gaze moved with rapid speed, analyzing what he saw at a terrifying pace. He picked out seams in the chaos. A flank where defenders pushed one step too far forward, focused on the undead press. A junction where three streets converged and command signals bottlenecked. A rooftop cluster sheltering healers with no rear coverage. A reserve force waiting just long enough to be late.
Opportunistic angles.
Backs turned. Lines stretched thin.

His mind worked faster than sight. The primordial brain residing within his skull unfolded the field into layers. Movement vectors. Reaction delays. Panic thresholds. He saw not what was happening, but what would happen a few breaths from now.
Then, he cast.
"[Awaken]."
The words left him quietly.
The Soul Reaper saber answered.

Blue flame along its edge intensified, growing brighter, tighter, drawn inward until it looked less like fire and more like compressed light. The weapon hummed in his grip, eager to release the souls contained within its Eternal Damnation storage.
And then...
Nothing.
No release. No explosion of soul soldiers outward.
The spell was live, but restrained.
Quinlan held it there, forcing the power to wait. The pressure climbed, coiling through his arm, across his shoulders, down his spine. His armor groaned softly under the strain.
He closed his eyes, yet the battlefield remained vivid in his mind.
Every point he had marked burned into his awareness, each one anchored by intent. He did not need to see them anymore. They were already his.
Quinlan swung.
It was a simple motion. One clean arc through empty air.
The flame exploded.
The saber's edge flared white-blue, and from it burst a cascade of light. More than a hundred sparks tore free, each one a tiny star shedding a thin tail of fire as it screamed downward.
From the walls below, defenders looked up.
For a heartbeat, some forgot to breathe. Such was the mesmerizing visage they saw.
The sky was falling apart, raining blue fire. It was beautiful in a distant, terrible way. A starfall aimed directly at the city.

Then the sparks exploded and began expanding rapidly, unfolding into forms. Flame pulled inward, condensing, stretching, hardening. Limbs shaped themselves out of burning light. Armor followed, seamless and cruel. Faces formed last, cold and ready to do what was ordered of them.
Quinlan opened his eyes.
"Kill them all."
The order was given by a deep voice that they all heard. It held zero mercy.
Blue-skinned warriors tore out of the fire.

They rose behind shield lines. They emerged from alley mouths. They solidified atop rooftops and dropped down into the midst of command units. Every place Quinlan had marked now had an Elite Soul standing there.
The humans who had stared upward in awe found themselves trapped.
Undead pressed from the front, relentless and uncaring.
And behind them...
These things.
The blue warriors raised their weapons in unison.
High above, Quinlan steadied himself.
The saber dimmed to a controlled burn at his side.
"[Necromantic Codex]," he called.
A book slid into existence, hovering in the air in front of him. Quinlan opened it with his will alone.
Pages turned on their own, stopping where he desired. Elite Souls: 180

Most of them had been added over the past few days. Quinlan has been incredibly productive in recent times, making use of the chaotic situation that enveloped the Vraven Kingdom, in large part due to his machinations.
Thousands had died by his hand or at his order.
His eyes moved to the top of the list.
Scar. Rank 5.
The only one.
Everything below her sat at Rank 4, or those he didn't manage to upgrade yet, due to just having finished their slaying, were below at Rank 1.

He focused on her entry, and the Codex responded, unfolding details. Her stat growth, while not able to be quantified as easily as it was for living beings, as Scar did not have a status window, she gained nearly equivalent to ten levels of stats. More important than that, her class had returned.
The real thing.

Rank 5 did that, making it the biggest boost in power among all the rank-ups thus far. It did not just strengthen: it restored. Scar was no longer an enhanced weapon. She was herself again, sharpened and elevated.
Quinlan closed that page and turned to another.
The restriction glared back at him, unchanged.
To ascend from Rank 4 to Rank 5, only Lesser Souls of level fifty or above were valid fuel. Anything weaker was rejected outright. Burned without effect.
That was the bottleneck. That was why Scar stood alone.
High-level enemies were rare. High-level enemies he could kill were even rarer.
Until Greyhaven.

chapters.title: Chapter 1379 More!
paragraphs: His gaze dipped toward the city as memory aligned with numbers. Officers. Veteran mages. Command staff. Elite guards who had survived more than one campaign. They fell to him or his soul army.
Yet, only a fraction of them rose as Elite Souls.
The rest became Lesser Souls.

Lesser Souls could be used as fighters... Casting [March of the Damned] allowed Quinlan to summon them, but only for a day. Once the twenty-four hours were up, they would become unusable, drifting back to the Goddess to rejoin Thalorind's soul ecosystem.
In a pinch, it was good to call on them. But in any other situation, using them like that would feel incredibly wasteful to Quinlan.
But that was not something he had to concern himself with, for there was a second use for those souls.
They made the perfect fuel.
"[Soul Fusion]," Quinlan called.
The Codex reacted instantly.
This was the largest mass upgrade Quinlan ever did, and the scale of it showed instantly.

Pages snapped forward and back in violent succession, no longer turning with calm intent but slamming against one another as if fighting to keep up. Columns of names blurred. Lines of soul count drained and refilled in rapid bursts. Symbols burned brighter, then dimmed, then brightened again as selections locked in.
Quinlan's eyes ignited.

Ghostly blue fire filled his gaze, spilling outward just enough to mark the air around his face. His pupils vanished beneath the glow. His breathing remained slow and controlled, but the space around him felt heavier.
He fused dozens of souls at once.
Then more.

Lesser Souls vanished from the Codex by the hundreds, stripped down to raw essence and funneled upward through invisible channels. The flow did not rush. It was precise. Metered. Every fragment was sent where it would produce the highest return.
Below, the battlefield reacted.
Elite Souls lit up mid-strike as blue light flooded through their forms. Stances adjusted on instinct that had not existed a moment earlier.
One of them dropped to a knee, weapon lowered.
"Master... I remember."
Another followed, gripping her spear with both hands as symbols ignited along its shaft.
"My class...!! It is back, just like it was for Lady Scar. Master blessed me with such a gift...! I can't believe it..." A tear of soul light dripped down her cheeks.
A third laughed once, short and sharp, then rolled his shoulders as if shaking off long stiffness.
"I can feel it. This is how it used to be."
The change rolled outward in waves.
The biggest shift came from the backline.
The mages.

Rank 4 and below mage souls had always been a giant compromise. They fought with raw output and limited patterns. Without classes, they couldn't cast spells. It made them, even at high Rank, much less useful than a lower-ranked physical-oriented soul soldier.
That limitation vanished.
A fire mage straightened with her staff flaring to life in her grip. Symbols burned into existence around her hands as spell frameworks locked back into place.
She thrust the staff forward and shouted with utmost exhilaration, "Burn and empower my master! [Fireball]!"
A column of fire slammed into a street choke point, punching through shields and armor alike.
Nearby, a lightning mage lifted both hands skyward.
"I call upon thee, my storm! Let me finally bring glory to my master! [Thunderbolt!]"
Clouds above the city twisted unnaturally, drawn into alignment. A moment later, lightning fell in a devastating strike, snapping down onto clustered defenders who had just turned to dodge.

Across the city, blue warriors moved with new coordination. Strikes landed cleaner. Archers shot with supernatural precision or power. Fighters struck with mana-empowered slashes that cut through armor. Units that had been dangerous became lethal.
This was not mere reinforcement... This was an elevation.
The soul army had been upgraded, reaching a new height.
High above them all, the Codex snapped shut.
Quinlan lowered his hand.
The glow in his eyes intensified as he looked down at the city he was harvesting.
Then his voice rolled outward.
Wind gathered at his back, carrying sound. Every street caught it. Every wall reflected it. Every defender heard it as clearly as those closest to him.
"More..." Quinlan began.
The word carried immense weight, an unnatural, gluttonous desire for more. "I need more."
Another breath. Another push of air.
"To upgrade all of you, I need more. To upgrade you further, I need more."
The wind rose higher, sharper now.
"To give you the comrades you deserve..."
"Need..."
His voice thickened, booming louder than ever before as he shouted,
"More!"
"So much more!"
His gaze swept the battlefield.
"So go, my soldiers!"
"Get me more!"
The wind carried the command through screams, through steel, through fire.
The defenders heard it too.
And for the first time since the siege began, some of them understood something with perfect clarity.
They were not fighting an army.
They were being processed.
But for the Elite Souls, the mood was vastly different. The command of their master settled into them.
Across streets choked with smoke, across rooftops slick with blood and broken tile, across alleys where light barely reached, the Elite Souls reacted the same way.
They smiled.
Not wide. Not manic.
Small, contained lifts at the corner of the mouth. A softening around the eyes. Familiar expressions worn by soldiers who had finally been given tools that let them do their work as they desired.
A swordsman stepped forward through falling ash, blade resting easy in his grip. His posture straightened, shoulders setting as if a long-carried weight had finally been adjusted properly.
A spearwoman twisted her weapon once, testing the balance she already knew was perfect. The faint glow along the haft steadied, responding to her touch like an old companion.
An archer nocked an arrow without looking, fingers moving on memory restored. Her breathing slowed, measured to the space between heartbeats.
Even the mages, newly awakened, shared the same look.
Understanding and approval.
Their master wanted more, and they would give it to him.
Then, as if drawn by a single thought, every Elite Soul turned their head upward for just a moment.
From hundreds of throats, from mouths that had not practiced together, from bodies scattered across the city's broken expanse, a single answer rose.
Loud and clear, boisterous enough to rattle windows and shake dust from ruined beams.
"Yes, Master!"

"Need..."
His voice thickened, booming louder than ever before as he shouted,
"More!"
"So much more!"
His gaze swept the battlefield.
"So go, my soldiers!"
"Get me more!"
The wind carried the command through screams, through steel, through fire.
The defenders heard it too.
And for the first time since the siege began, some of them understood something with perfect clarity.
They were not fighting an army.
They were being processed.
But for the Elite Souls, the mood was vastly different.
The command of their master settled into them.
Across streets choked with smoke, across rooftops slick with blood and broken tile, across alleys where light barely reached, the Elite Souls reacted the same way.
They smiled.
Not wide.
Not manic.
Small, contained lifts at the corner of the mouth.
A softening around the eyes.
Familiar expressions worn by soldiers who had finally been given tools that let them do their work as they desired.
A swordsman stepped forward through falling ash, blade resting easy in his grip.
His posture straightened, shoulders setting as if a long-carried weight had finally been adjusted properly.
A spearwoman twisted her weapon once, testing the balance she already knew was perfect.
The faint glow along the haft steadied, responding to her touch like an old companion.
An archer nocked an arrow without looking, fingers moving on memory restored.
Her breathing slowed, measured to the space between heartbeats.
Even the mages, newly awakened, shared the same look.
Understanding and approval.
Their master wanted more, and they would give it to him.
Then, as if drawn by a single thought, every Elite Soul turned their head upward for just a moment.
From hundreds of throats, from mouths that had not practiced together, from bodies scattered across the city's broken expanse, a single answer rose.
Loud and clear, boisterous enough to rattle windows and shake dust from ruined beams.
"Yes, Master!"

chapters.title: Chapter 1380 Lord of Farnath
paragraphs: "Yes, Master!"
The roar had not finished echoing when Lord Halveth of Farnath staggered back from the tall window of his keep.

His fingers scraped along the stone sill and missed purchase, grabbing onto nothing. As a result, his voluptuous behind hit the floor hard, releasing a far too loud thud. The sound of it seemed absurdly loud in the chamber. His breath came shallow, uneven, fogging the winter air as he stared back out at the sky.
High above the city, a dark figure hovered.

It did not move like a man. It did not float like a mage either. It simply remained there, fixed in place, as if the sky itself had decided to tolerate its presence. Around it, blue flames poured out, down into the streets and rooftops below, appearing where no unit should have been able to reach.
Then the shout's echo came again, bouncing between towers and alleys.
"Yes, Master!"
"What..." Halveth's face had drained of color.
Behind him stood three figures.

Elven slave girls. Tall, pale, dressed in loose robes that clung where they should not and hung open where dignity should have remained. The fabric was thin on purpose, marked with metal rings and cords meant to remind them of their place. Their long hair fell unbound down their backs. None of them reacted to the shout. None of them reacted to his falling. None even reacted to the ominous figure in the sky.
They simply stood.
Their eyes were open, but unfocused. Their posture was straight, but empty. They looked like decorations placed carefully behind their owner, arranged for display rather than presence.
Lord Halveth swallowed.

He had a wife. Still did, somewhere in the west wing, kept comfortable and quiet. She had done her duty years ago. Three children. An heir. That had been enough. Time had done the woman badly, with ugly wrinkles forming where he no longer wished to look.

Elves, on the other hand, stayed young. Buying one young elven girl was akin to purchasing a tool that would serve his family well for many generations. And if, after being bred with an elven male, she got pregnant... a fertile elven girl was essentially a money-printing machine. However, capturing an elven male was extremely difficult, as they never left their homes in Elvardia and were fiercely protected by their far stronger women.

And with Farnath sitting so close to the Elvardian border, acquiring them - both elven women and men - had been more than possible. Elven women came to Farnath of their own volition, pushing into Vraven to invade and take lands. Conducting a high-tier raiding party to grab a few males from the closest little villages wasn't too difficult either. This way, Halveth didn't even have to pay gold for them, as lords not living on the border had to. In fact, it was Halveth who conducted many of the auctions where elves and dwarves were sold further inward into the country.
However, now, that was no concern of the lord of Farnath.

The blue figures below moved with purpose. Streets that had held defenders moments ago were being erased. Units folded inward, swallowed between undead from the front and those things from behind. The city was coming apart in clean, methodical sections.
And above it all was that figure.
Halveth pushed himself up on one elbow and lifted a shaking hand, pointing through the window.
"W-what is that thing...?" he whispered.

His voice did not carry. "Hm!" But then, all of a sudden, Lord Halveth collected himself with a deep inhale and lurched upright. His balance wavered for a moment, then held. He spun on the three elves.
"You're standing there?" His voice was sharp and ugly, full of accusation, as if they had done something horribly wrong. "That's it? No tears? No trembling?"
He took two steps toward them, finger stabbing the right above their hearts.
"Are you happy?" he snarled. "After all these centuries, hm? Elvardia finally comes knocking. Bombarding my city. My walls. My streets."
They did not move.

"The king is nowhere to be seen. The duke either. I can't even call them." He laughed once, high and broken. "Some suppression magic, some clever trick. I bet the midgets are behind this. And my barrier." His hand clenched. "Gone."
He leaned in close.
"So tell me. Are you not happy?"
Nothing.
Not a flinch. Not a blink.
His lips twitched. His eyes began to dart.
"And now there's that thing in my skies." He turned back toward the window, then snapped around again, grin stretching too wide. "Wait. That looks like a man, doesn't it?"
A thin laugh slipped out.
"Elven men are weak. Everyone knows that. And he's far too tall to be a dwarf." His laugh grew louder, unsteady. "So maybe he's not with you at all. Maybe you're not getting saved."
His gaze spiraled, unfocused.

"Maybe he's with the undead," he went on, words tumbling faster now. "Maybe he'll capture you. Strap you down. Cut you open piece by piece." His hand gestured wildly. "Unholy experiments. Living test subjects. How does that sound?"
He stepped back, spreading his arms.
"Suddenly, I don't seem so bad, do I? I gave you a home, warmth, healthy meals, and companionship!" His voice rose again. "Yet you act like I was a cruel monster!"
He searched their faces, desperate for something. A tremor. A tightening of shoulders. Anything.
Halveth felt deathly scared, feeling the end was near. His life as he knew it was likely over. He wanted his women to mirror his deep fears, to not feel alone in this grave moment.
But there was nothing. They showed no emotions.
The silence pressed in.
Then the oldest of them moved.
She lifted her head.
Her eyes, once dull, focused. For the first time in centuries, she looked like a living being. Her mouth curved with intent that had been held down for far too long.
"If becoming a test subject for the undead ensures the fall of men like you, then it would be my honor to be useful."
Then, with a mocking curtsy of respect, she added, "Master."
The words landed hard.
Halveth's eyes stretched wide, whites showing. His mouth opened, then snapped shut, then opened again.
"Y-you- how dare you?! You show a sign of life after all this time, only to do this?!" He wanted to call her name, but he'd forgotten a long time ago. "Obey me!"
His hand rose, pulled back for a strong punch aimed right at her jaw.
It never connected.
Something shifted behind him.
Not sound. Not pressure. Something deeper, like the air itself, had decided to recoil.
Halveth froze.
Slowly, stiffly, he turned his head.
High above the city, the figure in the sky moved.
Just its head.
The motion was unhurried. Measured. As if time itself had been slowed to allow the gesture its full weight.
Two red orbs burned within the helm.
They locked onto him.
Halveth's throat seized.
"Hie!!" he screamed, the sound tearing out of him as his knees buckled beneath the gaze.
The figure vanished.
As far as Halveth's senses were concerned, it was simply gone.
The space it had occupied snapped empty, leaving only sky and falling ash.
Halveth sucked in a breath so sharp it burned. His head jerked side to side, eyes skittering across the window, the clouds, the broken skyline.
"W-where?!"
Panic broke what little structure his thoughts still had.
He lunged backward, stumbling into the elves, grabbing at silk and pale wrists with shaking hands. His body pressed in behind the eldest, using her as a shield without hesitation.
"Protect me!" he shrieked. "All of you! Offer up your lives!"

The words hit instantly. As their master, the owner of their lives due to their slave contracts having utterly zero clauses protecting their rights as living beings, he had the right to order them to slit their own throats should he wish to.
As such, the three elves moved.

They stepped forward in unison, bodies aligning without a word. The eldest took the center, feet braced, shoulders squared. The other two flanked her, half a step back, forming a shallow arc that placed their bodies squarely between Halveth and the open chamber.
Arms lifted. Palms turned outward.
Halveth crouched behind them, fingers digging into the back of the eldest's robe, knuckles white.
The command of her master wrapped around Vaelith's throat.

Her body moved before her thoughts finished forming. Muscles aligned. Weight settled into her heels. Arms lifted, palms open, empty, exposed. The position was wrong. Defensive without tools. Ritual without honor.
Inside, something folded.
Vaelith felt it the way one feels a hand closing around the throat while the lungs still work. Thought continued. Choice did not.
A tear never reached her eye. It slid inward, dissolving before it could become anything he might notice.
She knew.
She had known the moment the sky answered that man.
She had no chance.

chapters.title: Chapter 1381 Master's Order
paragraphs: Her bow was gone. It had been taken a long time ago, first locked away, then brought back out, only to be mocked. Strung wrong. Bent. Used as something to laugh at. A reminder that the things she had been proud of could be turned into tools for his amusement. Halveth had never liked women who were stronger than he was. So he made sure they never had the means to overpower him.
Now there was only her humiliating fabric between her and death.
It would not protect her from his attack one bit.
Her fists felt small when she clenched them. Light. Breakable. She tried to picture striking that thing in the sky. Tried to imagine bone meeting that ominous, black armor.
Her mind could not finish the image.
Her body reacted anyway.

Old habits clawed their way up from where they had been buried. Angles. Distance. Height. Unlike Halveth, her senses were far more acute and precise, letting Vaelith see the way the air had shifted when he vanished. He had not disappeared. She knew that with the same certainty she once knew wind before rain. He had gone higher, flying above the window, so they lost sight of him.
Hiding.
Her warrior instincts screamed to run. Every sense begged for it. Run. Scatter. Survive.
The slave magic tightened.
Her feet stayed planted.
Her mouth opened.
"I'll stay behind. You two, take Lord Halveth to the bunker and-"
The words jammed halfway out.
Sound reached her first.
Wet. Wrong.
A breath trying to escape through a throat that no longer worked.
She froze.
Behind her, something gurgled.
Lord Halveth was no longer behind her.
He was above her.

Stone had erupted from the floor in a jagged, brutal spike, thrusting up at a slanted angle. It had entered him between the legs, splitting fabric and flesh alike, and burst out through his throat. His mouth hung open around the rock, jaw forced wide, tongue pinned uselessly to one side. Blood ran down the stone in slow, uneven trails, dripping back onto the tiles he had once paced with authority.
His eyes bulged. Still alive. Barely.
Vaelith's breath caught.
'What...? When...?'

Her thoughts stumbled over themselves. There had been no warning. No sound of casting. No impact she could remember. One moment, Halveth had been clutching her robe. Next, he was impaled like a grotesque banner.
Her gaze snapped sideways.

He was there, seated on the sill of a far window. The dark armored man had not burst through stone or shattered walls to arrive. He simply entered through an open window, showing how lacking the internal defenses of the city were, relying on the barrier, manpower, and defensive artillery. Once inside, bypassing the military, Farnath showed little resistance. Now, the ominous entity was close enough that she could see the faint glow of red behind the visor.
Still.
Unhurried.
As if he had been there the entire time.
'So fast... So silent...' Vaelith murmured inwardly.
The slave magic surged again.

Despite the spike. Despite the blood. Despite the fact that their master was already dying, the command still held. Her body shifted, stepping back into position. The other two moved as well, flanking her automatically, placing themselves between the impaled man and the seated figure.
Protect.
At any cost.
The armored man did not rise. Did not draw a weapon. He watched them with nonchalant curiosity.
Vaelith felt it then.
A pulling sensation deep in her chest. A dimming. As if someone had turned down a lamp behind her eyes.
Her knees threatened to buckle.
She understood.

When a master died, bound slaves who had their contracts secured tightly did not gain freedom. Instead, they lost themselves. Consciousness faded, locking them in place until collection so that inheritance could happen, with another name replacing the old one on the contract.
But something told Vaelith that she would not be passed down to the next lord of Farnath.
Darkness crept in from the edges of her vision.
She forced herself to look at him one last time.
He should have been terrifying. Everything about him said danger. Power. Finality.
Instead, what met her heart was something else entirely.
Joy.
Her lips moved.
"Thank you..."
Then the world went dark.
Quinlan stayed seated for a breath longer.
The three elves lay where they had fallen, bodies slack, breathing shallow and even. Then he exhaled.
"As a slave master myself, I might not have the right to judge..."
His gaze shifted to Halveth's corpse.
"But man, what a cowardly piece of shit. I don't even want to claim your soul. It'd taint me."
Then he looked up toward the sky. "Lilyanna, you can have him."
Quinlan raised his hand and snapped his fingers.
The stone obeyed.

The pillar inside Havleth's corpse thickened in a slow swell. Rock pressed outward, expanding. Flesh stretched. Bone bowed. His spine arched, then failed. The sound was dull and wet, more pressure than impact.
Quinlan turned his wrist.
Wind answered.

A clean current wrapped around the three elves, lifting them just enough that their hair stirred and their robes shifted. The air carried them toward him, gentle and steady, and moved through the portal he summoned just now. Miri Town lay on the other side, sunlit and calm. Jasmine stood waiting for the new arrivals. As the governor of his lands, she's been very busy, and even more so since he began migrating thousands of slaves of various races over.
But the brunette merchant girl with big ambitions was more than ready for the challenge.
"Hm? Quin is already at work, I see," she smiled fondly while stepping forward, reaching out to hold the paralyzed ladies as they drifted through.
They were gone before the stone finished its work.
The pillar continued to expand.
Halveth's body gave way from the inside out. Armor split along seams never meant to bear outward force. What remained could not hold together. The stone reached its limit and stopped.
Then everything else failed.
The chamber was painted in a single violent moment. Walls. Pillars. The ornate carpet Halveth had commissioned himself.
Quinlan pushed his palm forward.
Wind slammed outward, hard and precise, forcing the spray of blood and innards away from him. Nothing touched his armor. Not a drop.
When the air settled, the pillar stood alone, thick and inert, its burden gone.
Quinlan rose from the windowsill at last.
He glanced once more at the empty space where the elves had been, then turned and flew out of the window, looking for his next prey.
And just like this, minutes passed. The terror of the man in the skies grew with each passing moment as he obliterated whole battalions while remaining near untouchable for the human defenders.

To resist, one needed to have the ability to conduct aerial warfare. The defenders of Farnath were simply not prepared for that, especially not while they had to contend with undead hordes, blue-skinned creatures - each of whom was now akin to walking one-man armies - the gang of ladies tearing their streets and walls up, as well as the Elvardian push that had reached the walls.
To fight back against Quinlan, simply throwing javelins at him was no longer enough. He'd grown far too powerful for such a crude method to restrict him.
And as a result, Farnath's fate had been sealed as soon as it became the Primordial Villain's next target.

I don't even want to claim your soul.
It'd taint me."
Then he looked up toward the sky.
"Lilyanna, you can have him."
Quinlan raised his hand and snapped his fingers.
The stone obeyed.
The pillar inside Havleth's corpse thickened in a slow swell.
Rock pressed outward, expanding.
Flesh stretched.
Bone bowed.
His spine arched, then failed.
The sound was dull and wet, more pressure than impact.
Quinlan turned his wrist.
Wind answered.
A clean current wrapped around the three elves, lifting them just enough that their hair stirred and their robes shifted.
The air carried them toward him, gentle and steady, and moved through the portal he summoned just now.
Miri Town lay on the other side, sunlit and calm.
Jasmine stood waiting for the new arrivals.
As the governor of his lands, she's been very busy, and even more so since he began migrating thousands of slaves of various races over.
But the brunette merchant girl with big ambitions was more than ready for the challenge.
"Hm?
Quin is already at work, I see," she smiled fondly while stepping forward, reaching out to hold the paralyzed ladies as they drifted through.
They were gone before the stone finished its work.
The pillar continued to expand.
Halveth's body gave way from the inside out.
Armor split along seams never meant to bear outward force.
What remained could not hold together.
The stone reached its limit and stopped.
Then everything else failed.
The chamber was painted in a single violent moment.
Walls.
Pillars.
The ornate carpet Halveth had commissioned himself.
Quinlan pushed his palm forward.
Wind slammed outward, hard and precise, forcing the spray of blood and innards away from him.
Nothing touched his armor.
Not a drop.
When the air settled, the pillar stood alone, thick and inert, its burden gone.
Quinlan rose from the windowsill at last.
He glanced once more at the empty space where the elves had been, then turned and flew out of the window, looking for his next prey.
And just like this, minutes passed.
The terror of the man in the skies grew with each passing moment as he obliterated whole battalions while remaining near untouchable for the human defenders.
To resist, one needed to have the ability to conduct aerial warfare.

The defenders of Farnath were simply not prepared for that, especially not while they had to contend with undead hordes, blue-skinned creatures - each of whom was now akin to walking one-man armies - the gang of ladies tearing their streets and walls up, as well as the Elvardian push that had reached the walls.
To fight back against Quinlan, simply throwing javelins at him was no longer enough.
He'd grown far too powerful for such a crude method to restrict him.
And as a result, Farnath's fate had been sealed as soon as it became the Primordial Villain's next target.

chapters.title: Chapter 1382 Final Push
paragraphs: Boots hammered stone in a loose, breaking rhythm.

No formation held. Shields banged into backs. Someone tripped and went down hard. No one stopped for him. Hands and feet shoved him aside without looking. Bodies collided as the street narrowed and widened again between leaning buildings.
Breath tore out of lungs in sharp bursts. Throats burned. Armor straps cut into the shoulders with every step.
"Move!" someone shouted with a raw voice. "Move, move!"
"Hurry, or we're done for!"
A glance over a shoulder.

The sky above the rooftops held a dark shape that closed the distance without effort. Unlike them, it did not have to weave through obstacles. Rooflines fell away beneath it. Smoke parted around it and the red flames its obsidian armor emitted.
A javelin flew.
It arced high, wobbled, then fell short and clattered uselessly across tiles.
Someone laughed, thin and hysterical. "Haha! When does this dream end?! Someone slap me awake!"
"Mommy...!" Someone else sobbed without slowing.
They ran harder.
The street opened into a small square littered with debris and broken carts. A bottleneck. Too wide to hide. Too open to scatter.
The sound came first.
Air compressed with a deep, crushing pressure that shoved at their backs. Shadows snapped tight beneath their feet.
The figure dropped down on them like a falling meteor, and instantly, it exploded.

Stone shattered on impact. The ground caved inward in a violent ring. Men were lifted off their feet as if yanked by invisible hooks. Armor folded. Bodies collided midair. Limbs bent where they should not.

The force rolled outward through the square, ripping through the cluster in a single breath. Those closest vanished into fragments of plate and flesh. Those farther out slammed into walls hard enough to leave stains where they hit.
Dust filled mouths and eyes.
The square fell silent.

When it cleared, nothing moved. Broken weapons lay half-buried in rubble. Shields rested at angles that made no sense. What had been a unit moments ago was reduced to scattered remains pressed into the ground and walls.

Quinlan straightened his spine while standing in the crater of his own creation. "Thanks, Synchra," he muttered, always grateful for the protection of his trusted armor. She was doing incredible work. Synchra granted Quinlan plainly unfair levels of tankiness, which in turn made him able to approach combat from a different angle. Before, most of these combatants would've been strong enough to one-shot kill him if their strike connected. But that was no longer the case.
Synchra's red flames rose in response to the praise she received, joyous.
It felt great to be noticed for the hard work she was putting in.
Quinlan's gaze moved once, left to right, counting shapes that twitched or dragged themselves an inch at a time. His hand lifted.
Compressed water snapped into existence at his fingertips, each shot a tight cylinder that bent the air around it. He flicked his wrist.
*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

The bullets punched through helms and throats with clean, short sounds. One man tried to crawl. The next shot folded him flat against the stones. Another raised an arm. Water took it off at the elbow and kept going.

Quinlan tilted his head to the side, watching the futile resistance of his targets. At the same time, he listened to the symphony of alert notifications, his favorite music these days, ringing in his mind.
[Ding!]
[You've reached Level 48.]
He smiled as the last shots landed and the mass execution was completed.
"Amazing," he murmured.

He glanced at the numbers without slowing, eyes tracking the rise. In a single day, the gain eclipsed entire campaigns. Even the lionkin genocide he conducted in Lionheart with the temporary tenfold boost had not climbed this fast. His growing power level, bolstered defenses, and increased proficiency with his magic had changed what was possible. Now, unlike how it was back in Lionheart, his spells were strong enough to kill high-rank targets. Furthermore, he was attacking whole settlements that were full of them, using the blood, time, and money of his newfound allies to his full advantage. It was Elvardia and the Covenant who spent numerous years preparing for this invasion.
It was Elvardia and the Covenant who spent immense resources to make this invasion possible.
It was Elvardia and the Covenant who were now bleeding in the fields.
But it was Quinlan who was reaping the biggest benefits.
Thanks to the hard work of his allies, level fifty was no longer a distant goal to chase. It hovered close, almost close enough to touch.
Quinlan rose out of the crater, lifting high into the air.
One look was enough. The same pattern.

In Greyhaven, it had been the same. The first crush erased the center. Command collapsed. Cohesion died. What remained were fragments. Small knots of soldiers clinging to alleys, doorways, and courtyards. Scattered prey instead of an army.
His eyes traced movement along rooftops and side streets. No dense clusters. No clean follow-ups.
It was no longer worth Quinlan's time. His more than 200 Elite Souls would do the hard work for him.
"Time for plan B."
He flicked two fingers.
Space peeled open on the roof of a tall building overlooking the square. The tear stabilized into a clean-edged portal, light folding inward around it.
A nun stepped through.
She wore round glasses that caught the glow of the remnants of his explosion, and freckles dusted across her cheeks. Mira took two confident steps forward, hands clasped behind her back as she spoke.
"Well then," she said cheerfully, "looks like it's time for me to shine again, hmm, Mister Villain? The terror of the kingdom needs the help of this humble little nun-"
Her foot met empty air.
She blinked once.
Then gravity remembered her.
"CATCH ME, YOU MOTHERFU-"
She dropped.

Arms windmilled. Legs kicked at nothing. Her body twisted, fighting an argument it could not win. The roof slid past above her. The ground rushed up, filling her vision, stone details snapping into sharp focus far too fast.
Her face was an inch from impact.
Wind wrapped around her torso.
The fall stopped.
Momentum vanished as if cut clean. Mira was then jerked upward and slammed gently into solid arms. Quinlan caught her against his chest, one hand braced at her back, the other under her knees.
She stared at him with her glasses crooked and breath coming fast.
"I hate you!" she whined, gripping the front of his armor. "Stop having fun at my expense!"
"Stop worshipping a hypocrite, and I'll consider it."
Mira's face flushed with righteous outrage.

She twisted in his arms just enough to draw back a fist. "You shameless, heretical menace! You're but a villain speaking ill of the Maker! Do you have any idea how much divine retribution you're lining up for yourself?! I'm shocked she didn't smite you down already!"
Then Mira gasped. "Ah! Wait! Maybe I'm the divine retribution she sent to get you in line! Take this!"
She went for a slap.
*Thunk.*
The sound was dull. Solid.
A sharp jolt ran up her arm.
"Ouchhhh!"
Mira recoiled instantly, clutching her hand to her chest, hopping once in midair despite still being held. Her glasses slid further down her nose.
"Ow ow ow ow! You hurt me... Such a brutal sadist..." she whimpered, blinking at him rapidly with accusatory eyes while massaging her hand.
"Women..." Quinlan shook his head with a loud sigh escaping his lips.
"What?!" "A woman and a blind believer... The most delusional combination possible."
"I'm not delusional but aware! You're the one in the wrong!" Mira cried while massaging her poor hand.

"You know, I can't help but notice that the women of Thalorind, mostly you, like to call me a motherfucker. What gives? I mean, I might've sucked on the boobies of my mothers so strong that they orgasmed a little, but-"
"What's wrong with you?" Mira deadpanned.
Quinlan smirked, dismissing her whole existence. "Nothing, of course. I'm perfectly healthy in both body and mind. So, Miss Delulu with the Fist of Divine Retribution, shall we get started?"
Mira puffed her cheeks with lips pressed into a thin line. She glared at the smooth obsidian curve of his helmet.
"Wipe that smug smirk off your face," she muttered.
"What do you mean? You can't see my face."
"I can tell."
There was no pause. No protest.
"Is that so?"
He did not deny it.

chapters.title: Chapter 1383 Time Passes Until... Ding!
paragraphs: Her glare sharpened. Her shoulders drew up as she hugged her sore hand closer to her chest. "I hate you so damn much..."
The words came out small, tight, and sincere.
Quinlan laughed. It was a lot of fun to mess with this expressive nun.
But then, his laugh faded as abruptly as it began. "Alright. I think I've bullied you enough for now."
Mira only pouted harder, cheeks rounding even more as she turned her face away from him.
He shifted his grip.
Then he tossed her.
"Wha-!"
Her yelp cut off as Quinlan kicked off the air and caught her on his back.
"Hold on," he said nonchalantly.
She scrambled, arms locking around his neck, legs hooking at his sides. "You're the worst! I bet that when you greet the Goddess, she'll slap you, too! And that time, you'll feel it!"
"My mommies will protect me."
"Huh?"
They took off.
Orphanages were cleared one after another.
Every time, it was the same. Fear behind the door. Whispers. Prayers cut short when his presence was felt.
Then Mira stepped forward and quickly, briefly, explained what they had to know.
Wide eyes stared up at Quinlan's armor, then flicked back to her face. The tension eased just enough.
Children were gathered and passed into the waiting arms on the other side of the portal. Some were nuns, others were women and mothers.

Many of the original citizens of Miri Town were peasants who were driven to such poverty that they had to go rogue and join the Wraithclaws, which was a criminal organization that terrorized a few villages.
Quinlan conquered it and relocated the willing people to Miri Town.

As a result of their poverty and risky lives, many women had no children. Either due to sickness, malnutrition, stress, or a myriad of other effects. Now, those same women were treating these rapidly arriving orphans as pure blessings.
Just like that, one by one, the city emptied of them.
Mira stood alone at the edge of the portal.
Light spilled around her feet. The sounds of the city felt distant now, dulled and pushed aside. She did not turn to leave right away. Her hands came together at her waist. Her shoulders settled.
Then she bowed.
It was deep. Proper. Not rushed.
"Thank you for letting me do this, Quinlan Elysiar."
Quinlan watched her for a moment. "You thanked me last time, too."
She straightened and looked at him. There was no flare, no puffed cheeks, no sharp retort waiting behind her teeth.
"And I will thank you each and every time. Even if you do it a hundred times."
That gave him pause.
Quinlan's gaze lingered on her longer than before. Then he spoke quietly. "So you like it there."

Mira nodded. "Yes. It's only been a few minutes, but..." She glanced back through the portal. Although the nun couldn't see through with her eyes, her mind told her all she needed to know. Shapes moved on the other side. Women guiding children, who were already starting to regain their laughter despite being besieged by unholy monstrosities mere moments ago. "I can feel it just from the air. These people are kind beings. And Jasmine is a woman who takes her role seriously... I can tell that corrupting a governor like her will be near impossible. I feel hopeful about the future of Miri Town and its residents."
"Good," Quinlan said.
She smiled at him then. Small. Careful. No teeth. No hiss waiting behind it.

"G-good luck," Mira said, prompting Quinlan to raise an eyebrow. She knew he was a villain, here to kill human soldiers. Yet she, a nun, a devout follower of the Goddess, wished him good luck. Granted, there was nothing in the scriptures about human supremacy per se, for the Goddess loved all equally. But over time, most such motions were thrown aside. All races believed themselves to be the chosen ones, the favorites.
That's why her words carried immense weight.
Then she turned and stepped through the portal.
It closed behind her, leaving Quinlan alone in the city once more.
Next came the slave quarters.
His girls were already there.

The fighting had passed through the district hard and fast. Doors hung open. Chains lay coiled on floors where keys had been forced into hands. A few overseers knelt in lines with their wrists bound behind them, guarded by silent figures that did not breathe.
The contracts were stacked on a broken table. All accounted for.
They had done exactly what he expected.
Quinlan moved.
House by house. Yard by yard.

Locks gave way. Sigils burned out. The pressure that had sat on chests for years lifted in uneven waves. Some slaves fell to their knees. Some backed away from him in silence. Some stared at their hands as if waiting for the pain to return.
It did not.
Humans. Elves. Dwarves. Beastkin with collars worn thin from years of rubbing against skin.
Quinlan did not address them alone.

Seraphiel stepped forward for the elves. She spoke of the Lumi Forest that wrapped around Miri Town. Untainted nature. Clean water. Open paths beneath wide canopies. At times, Sylvaris stood beside her. Her presence drew murmurs. Some captives recognized her by name or by face, and the weight of her standing carried the words even further.

Felicity, sometimes accompanied by Ayame or Lucille, two dukes' daughters, addressed the humans. But it was the young princess who carried the show. She bowed first. She said her family had failed them. She did not soften it. She offered no orders, only a path forward. A city is being built far from her family's reach.

Kitsara took the beastkin who lingered at the edges. She spoke to the sharper-eyed ones first, the quick thinkers, the ones who watched from behind others. Terms. Opportunity. Space to breathe and live without chains. When that left gaps, Blossom filled them. The dogkin stood close to Quinlan, back straight, tail energetic. She spoke plainly. She spoke of him. What he did. How he treated those who stood with him. Her steady presence said the rest. For those who valued simple truths, it was enough.
Only the dwarves remained.
Quinlan stepped in himself.

He talked numbers. Metal quality. Booze access. Trade routes. He talked about the smithies already planned, about ore coming in steadily. About a drink that did not need to be watered down to stretch the supply. About a place where their work would not be claimed by another name.
He negotiated.
Some hesitated. Many did not.
Quinlan did not rush them.
Then the horns sounded again.
Another city followed. Another siege. Another massacre.
He rose back into the air.
More orphanages. More slave districts. The same pattern, repeated until the next cities felt hollowed out as well. Each siege fed the next. Each assault brought him XP and a growing soul army.
Elvardia and the Covenant bled.
Quinlan and his girls harvested.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until the sound returned.
[Ding!]
[XP threshold reached. Pass the Primordial Rank-Up Mission to proceed into the level 50s.]

The long-awaited mission was here, ready to begin immediately. However, this time, it would be nothing like Quinlan could've predicted. No Zhenwu-like lengthy escapades into other worlds, nor Iris-like simulations lasting years. It would be something new. Something shocking.

They had done exactly what he expected.
Quinlan moved.
House by house.
Yard by yard.
Locks gave way.
Sigils burned out.
The pressure that had sat on chests for years lifted in uneven waves.
Some slaves fell to their knees.
Some backed away from him in silence.
Some stared at their hands as if waiting for the pain to return.
It did not.
Humans.
Elves.
Dwarves.
Beastkin with collars worn thin from years of rubbing against skin.
Quinlan did not address them alone.
Seraphiel stepped forward for the elves.
She spoke of the Lumi Forest that wrapped around Miri Town.
Untainted nature.
Clean water.
Open paths beneath wide canopies.
At times, Sylvaris stood beside her.
Her presence drew murmurs.
Some captives recognized her by name or by face, and the weight of her standing carried the words even further.
Felicity, sometimes accompanied by Ayame or Lucille, two dukes' daughters, addressed the humans.
But it was the young princess who carried the show.
She bowed first.
She said her family had failed them.
She did not soften it.
She offered no orders, only a path forward.
A city is being built far from her family's reach.
Kitsara took the beastkin who lingered at the edges.
She spoke to the sharper-eyed ones first, the quick thinkers, the ones who watched from behind others.
Terms.
Opportunity.
Space to breathe and live without chains.
When that left gaps, Blossom filled them.
The dogkin stood close to Quinlan, back straight, tail energetic.
She spoke plainly.
She spoke of him.
What he did.
How he treated those who stood with him.
Her steady presence said the rest.
For those who valued simple truths, it was enough.
Only the dwarves remained.
Quinlan stepped in himself.
He talked numbers.
Metal quality.
Booze access.
Trade routes.
He talked about the smithies already planned, about ore coming in steadily.
About a drink that did not need to be watered down to stretch the supply.
About a place where their work would not be claimed by another name.
He negotiated.
Some hesitated.
Many did not.
Quinlan did not rush them.
Then the horns sounded again.
Another city followed.
Another siege.
Another massacre.
He rose back into the air.
More orphanages.
More slave districts.
The same pattern, repeated until the next cities felt hollowed out as well.
Each siege fed the next.
Each assault brought him XP and a growing soul army.
Elvardia and the Covenant bled.
Quinlan and his girls harvested.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until the sound returned.
[Ding!]
[XP threshold reached.
Pass the Primordial Rank-Up Mission to proceed into the level 50s.]
The long-awaited mission was here, ready to begin immediately.
However, this time, it would be nothing like Quinlan could've predicted.
No Zhenwu-like lengthy escapades into other worlds, nor Iris-like simulations lasting years.
It would be something new.
Something shocking.

chapters.title: Chapter 1384 Turbulent Alliance
paragraphs: The chamber was built for permanence.

Black stone walls rose in clean angles, etched with runes that marked treaties older than several mountain ranges. These were mostly treaties between tribes of the same race, for the Elvardian Alliance between the dwarves and elves was a more recent event, only a couple of tens of thousands of years old. A circular table of pale rootwood sat at the center, its surface unmarred by blades or cups. It was a place meant for decisions, not comfort.

Queen Myrasyn sat at its edge with her hands folded within the sleeves of her robe. Blonde hair fell straight down her back, bound by a simple clasp. Her gaze rested on the sigil circle carved into the table, calm and distant, as if the world beyond it moved on a slower rhythm.
King Ragnar remained seated on his raised throne. Broad shoulders filled the carved chair that had been shaped with him in mind.

The two rulers were in the strategy room, surrounded by their most trusted generals and advisors, overlooking the board as the invasion occurred in real time, using dwarven artifacts to signal the locations of each army.
Suddenly, the communication circle flared.
Light sank inward instead of spreading out, folding space until four shapes resolved across from them. Cold rot clung to the air, heavy and damp, like the breath of deep caverns and flooded crypts.
The first voice tore through the chamber before any greeting could settle.
"He keeps stealing!" the Drowned King screeched. "Stealing, lying, denying, smirking, and stealing again! On repeat! Again and again!"
"We, at the Covenant of Eternity, find the attitude of that man unacceptable," Archlich Vozen spoke up. "And the attitude of Elvardia even more unacceptable."
"That's right! Are you in cahoots with them, you snobby-"
"Silence," Queen Myrasyn ordered.
The word cut through the chamber like a blade laid flat against a throat.
The Drowned King froze mid-breath. His hollow sockets flicked sideways, as if testing whether he had truly heard her correctly.
The pause stretched.
Then Archlich Vozen leaned forward, which made the gems along his chain chime softly. His voice scraped out, dry and carrying the echo of burial chambers.

"You are not to order us around, elven queen." His skull tilted, empty eye lights flaring brighter. "Do not forget that your predecessor, who underestimated us, suffered a truly unfortunate accident. Kekeke..."
The Drowned King's laughter followed in the form of ear-scraping, raspy sounds.
Myrasyn's gaze sharpened. The calm distance drained from her eyes, replaced by something narrow and focused. Her posture did not change, but the air around her felt thinner, tighter.
"So you accept responsibility?" she asked.

Vozen waved one skeletal hand dismissively. "Me? Of course not. It was the work of a rogue lich, as we've been telling you for thousands of years. A tragic incident, really. The Covenant had nothing to do with it." His head tilted again. "But perhaps they learned of your predecessor's... horrible attitude toward our kind."
The temperature in the chamber dropped another degree. Several advisors shifted their footing. A dwarven general's jaw tightened.
King Ragnar spoke up at last.
"What do you want? Who keeps stealing?"

Vozen's jaw creaked as it opened again. He did not need to move his mouth to speak, for he had no vocal cords to make use of. All of it happened using his undead core, the unholy magic that kept his bones and soul together. Despite that, some liches retained habits of their old lives, which led some of them to make human-like motions out of instinct. Parting their lips when speaking, articulating words, was one such instinct. "I did not know the firm King Ragnar had become such a great actor."
Ragnar exhaled slowly through his nose. "The Primordial Villain."
The silence that followed was brief and brittle.

"Indeed!" the Drowned King snapped, surging to his feet. He stalked forward until his hollow, lifeless face filled the projection circle, water sloshing violently from his armor. "That thieving scum has the gall to steal our spoils of war from right under our noses! It is so obvious, and he still has the gall to deny it!"
Myrasyn's voice slipped in, soft and cold.
"Isn't that called karma?"
The Drowned King's head jerked toward her. "Shut your foul mouth—"
"Sit yourself down."
The command did not come from the elven queen this time.
It came from behind the lich.

The Blind Grave Oracle's voice was pale and flat, carrying none of the laziness it had held earlier. The Drowned King stiffened. He leaned back from the artifact slowly, disbelief rippling through his posture.
He turned.
The third figure came into focus.

She had been sitting motionless on her throne since the call began, spine straight, hands resting atop a staff grown from fused bone and black crystal. Her crown was simple, angular, set low against a skull etched with deep, deliberate runes. There was no excess adornment, no idle motion. Yet immense power clung to her nonetheless. Just looking at this undead monster was unnerving, enough to make seasoned warriors tremble and abandon their comrades as they ran in the opposite direction from her.
The Drowned King recoiled half a step, then bristled. "You do not get to order me around either!" he snapped. "Do not forget yourself. We are equals!"
The Blind Grave Oracle remained still as she decreed, "Equals in rank, perhaps."
Then her gaze lifted. "But in strength...?"
The Drowned King recoiled.

It was not a dramatic step. His foot slid back a fraction while his shoulders drew in despite himself. It had been a very long time since he had seen that lich direct anything resembling animosity at him.
"I-I'm powerful," he declared, forcing the words out with a rasp that scraped raw stone. "You know that. I have drowned cities under the weight of my mighty armies! I have-"
His voice faltered.
He stared into her face.

There was nothing there. No flare of ego. No irritation. No threat sharpened for display. Just an empty skull held perfectly still, runes etched deep enough that even time had failed to soften them. The sensation crept in without warning. Weight. Pressure. A sense of scale so vast it made his own years of corrupting this plane of existence feel thin and poorly justified. "The origin of your moniker. Have you forgotten?"
Unlike younger liches, she carried none of her past self. No lingering instincts made her act even remotely like a living being. She was a cold, unfeeling creature that should not be.

"!!" Suddenly, the memory of a human king leading his forces down a river surfaced. The boats carrying his mighty armies were drowned in the water when a single, horrible monstrosity stood in their way and showed him the power of corruption.
It'd been so long ago that the Drowned King had forgotten how he became an undead in the first place.
He felt small.
"You're an embarrassment," the Blind Grave Oracle added.
The words landed stronger than any punch could've.
The Drowned King's jaw worked soundlessly. His hands curled, then unclenched. After a long, grinding second, he turned away and lowered himself back onto his throne with stiff, jerking movements.
"This isn't over," he hissed. "I won't forget this."
The Blind Grave Oracle did not look at him again.
Her attention shifted through the projection, past the Covenant's chamber, and into the strategy room of Elvardia. Her unseen gaze settled on the two rulers across the table.
King Ragnar straightened. "A voice of reason, finally."
